query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high‐entropy alloys, the ability to form and retain a stable, coherent, slow‐growing protective oxide layer above 900 °C is governed by the uniform distribution of the minor X element (Al, Si, or Mn) within a single‐phase solid solution. This homogeneous composition enables preferential oxidation of X to form a continuous, adherent oxide (such as Al2O3 or SiO2) that matches the thermal expansion of the underlying alloy, minimizing stress. In contrast, multiphase alloys with compositional segregation lead to discontinuous oxide formation, local stress concentrations, and ultimately cracking or spallation of the protective scale.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy produced in either a single-phase (homogeneous solid solution) or multiphase state with possible segregation of the X element.
generation.intervention: Exposure of the alloy to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C for prolonged durations.
generation.conditions: High-temperature (≥900 °C) controlled oxidizing/corrosive environment where both temperature and oxygen activity are maintained constant.
generation.structural_mediator: The microstructural distribution and partitioning of the minor element X that forms the protective oxide, along with the phase homogeneity (single-phase vs multiphase) in the alloy.
generation.mechanism: In a homogeneous (single-phase) alloy, the minor X element preferentially migrates to the surface and oxidizes to form a slow-growing, coherent, adherent protective oxide layer. This layer has a thermal expansion more closely matched to the substrate, reducing interfacial stresses. In multiphase alloys, segregation of X or the presence of secondary phases causes an inhomogeneous oxide scale with varying thickness and properties, leading to localized stress concentrations and eventual cracking/spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under high-temperature exposure, single-phase CrFeCoNiX alloys will demonstrate a slow, parabolic oxide growth kinetics with a continuous, adherent oxide layer, while multiphase alloys will show faster, possibly breakaway oxidation kinetics with evidence of oxide cracking and spallation.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the behavior observed in multiphase CrFeCoNiX alloys that have previously exhibited cracking and spallation of their surface oxides.
generation.boundary: Test conditions are temperatures above 900 °C in oxidative/corrosive atmospheres for durations sufficient to observe long-term oxide growth (e.g., 50-200 hours).
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty remains in quantifying the exact diffusion rates of X within different microstructures and in determining the precise oxide compositions (e.g., relative stability of Al2O3 vs SiO2 vs Mn-oxides) under these conditions. The interplay between elemental partitioning and residual stresses across interfaces could also vary with slight deviations in composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrFeCoNiX alloy samples: one processed to obtain a single-phase, homogenized microstructure and another intentionally processed to generate a multiphase/microsegregated structure. Subject both sets to identical oxidative/corrosive conditions above 900 °C for extended periods. Use in-situ thermogravimetric analysis combined with post-exposure surface characterization (SEM/EDS, XRD) to evaluate oxide thickness, scale continuity, and presence of cracks/spallation.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and morphology (SEM, TEM)
Phase composition at the scale-substrate interface (XRD, EDS)
Surface stress or adhesion measurements (e.g., using scanning Kelvin probe)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the single-phase and multiphase samples develop similarly coherent, slow-growing oxide scales with no significant difference in adhesion or cracking behavior under identical test conditions, then the hypothesis that microstructural homogeneity controls protective oxide formation would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Oxidation behavior of a refractory AlNbTiVZr 0.25 high-entropy alloy at 600–900 °C was investigated. At 600–700 °C, two-stage oxidation kinetics was found: Nearly parabolic oxidation (n = 0.46–0.48) at the first stage, transitioned to breakaway oxidation (n = 0.75–0.72) at the second stage. At 800 °C, the oxidation kinetics was nearly linear (n = 0.92) throughout the entire duration of testing. At 900 °C, the specimen disintegrated after 50 h of testing. The specific mass gains were estimated to be 7.2, 38.1, and 107.5, and 225.5 mg/cm 2 at 600, 700, and 800 °C for 100 h, and 900 °C for 50 h, respectively. Phase compositions and morphology of the oxide scales were analyzed using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). It was shown that the surface layer at 600 °C consisted of the V 2 O 5 , VO 2 , TiO 2 , Nb 2 O 5 , and TiNb 2 O 7 oxides. Meanwhile, the scale at 900 °C comprised of complex TiNb 2 O 7 , AlNbO 4 , and Nb 2 Zr 6 O 17 oxides. The oxidation mechanisms operating at different temperatures were discussed and a comparison of oxidation characteristics with the other alloys was conducted. Abstract Although refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO 4 -based oxide with some dispersion of Al 2 O 3 and Cr 2 O 3 . At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm 2 , which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date.
